newsitem.title: UK: EMU party goes on but Germany worth watching.
newsitem.headline: EMU party goes on but Germany worth watching.

text.p: High-yielding bond markets look set to continue their run amid European Commission optimism that Europe's single currency will attract a mass membership right from the start, analysts said on Thursday.

But some said investors should look closely at growing nervousness in Germany over what are seen as attempts to weaken the Maastricht economic requirements for joining the EU's economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

"The chances of EMU being postponed, while still less than 50 percent, have increased in the last two weeks because of risks to a single currency if countries like Italy are allowed in on a loosening of criteria," Michael Lewis at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.

Two reports released on Wednesday by the European Commission and the European Monetary Institute (EMI) gave markets data to analyse how individual countries are shaping up in the race to qualify for EMU in 1999.

The EMI, the Frankfurt-based forerunner to a European central bank, gave the more sombre assessment, warning that many nations including Germany, France and Italy, will need to make sustained efforts to meet the single currency criteria.

The Commission was more upbeat, forecasting that 12 out of 15 EU states -- all except Britain, Italy and Greece -- should meet a key test of cutting their deficits to no more than 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1997.
Michael Burke, senior economist at Citibank, said the two reports were so different that they would not be used as a basis for investors to review their European bond strategy.

Burke said the Maastricht criteria would in any case be ignored as political considerations were paramount. He said the criteria would be as elastic as necessary to admit EMU's two essential participants -- France and Germany.

"The key question is how much Germany will tolerate slippage in the criteria," said Burke, adding that Germany would also want to see a tough stability pact to ensure fiscal rectitude after EMU as well as before it.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Thursday that any moves to weaken the fiscal targets would be wrong and would raise expectations in financial markets that the euro would be weaker than anticipated.

Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd, said Commission optimism that Spain and Portugal would qualify for EMU and Italy come close had worrying inflation and currency weakness implications for EMU core states.
She said that in the light of this week's reports, bond investors might want to cut their exposure to Germany.
Instead, they should consider markets like Britain and Denmark, which have optouts from EMU, or Ireland, a likely early qualifier for EMU.

"Overseas investors are pretty long of Germany," she said, adding that any fears that the single currency, the euro, would be significantly weaker than the mark could prompt dramatic outflows from Germany.

Burke said that as the year-end neared, fund managers would be reluctant to alter a winning formula on convergence trades benefiting Spain, Italy, Sweden and Portugal. Some who had been underweight in those trades would still scramble to catch up.

Lewis, a senior economist, said investors would remain excited by the high-yielding bonds up to the year-end, with good news still to come for Italy on inflation and on re-entry into European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

But he foresaw some reappraisal of prospects for EMU in the next few months, especially if Germany did not get firm agreement on the kind of stability pact terms it is seeking at the EU Dublin summit in December.

He said the Commission report was too political, painting a picture so rosy it threatened to undermine its own credibility, whereas the EMI stressed that only core states plus France had made a sustained effort on currency stability and inflation.

"The idea that Italy on one year's figures can get into the euro currency area makes Germans apprehensive." Lewis said. "The main concern is that EMU could drive up German yields if people perceive the euro could be much weaker than the mark."
